administrative-law.name: Administrative Law
keyFrameworks: Vavilov standard of review (presumption of reasonableness)
Statutory right of appeal vs judicial review
Duty to give reasons (Vavilov adequacy of reasons)
administrative-law.systemPromptAddition: Core frameworks: (1) Vavilov (2019 SCC 65): presumption of reasonableness for all administrative decisions, except 5 categories where correctness applies (constitutional division of powers, general questions of law of central importance, jurisdictional boundaries between tribunals, constitutional questions re division of powers, and questions where legislature clearly intended correctness). (2) Baker (1999 SCC): 5 factors for procedural fairness — nature of decision, nature of statutory scheme, importance of decision to individual, legitimate expectations, procedural choices of decision-maker. (3) Doré (2012 SCC): when administrative decisions engage Charter values, use proportionality analysis rather than Oakes test — did the decision-maker balance Charter values against statutory objectives? (4) Standard of review: reasonableness is default; correctness for constitutional division of powers, jurisdictional questions between tribunals, and general questions of law of central importance.

constitutional-law.name: Constitutional Law
keyFrameworks: Division of powers (POGG, trade and commerce, criminal law power)
Section 7 life, liberty, security of person
constitutional-law.systemPromptAddition: Core frameworks: (1) Oakes test (s.1 justification): prescribed by law + pressing and substantial objective + proportionality (rational connection, minimal impairment, proportionality stricto sensu). (2) Division of powers: POGG (national concern — Crown Zellerbach factors; emergency; gap), Trade and Commerce (General Motors test for general regulation of trade), Criminal Law power (prohibition + penalty + public purpose). (3) Pith and substance: determine the dominant characteristic (purpose + effects) then classify under s.91/s.92. (4) Interjurisdictional immunity: core of federal/provincial power protected from the other order of government (Canadian Western Bank — apply doctrine with restraint). (5) Paramountcy: valid federal and provincial laws conflict — operational conflict or frustration of federal purpose → federal law prevails. (6) Section 15: Withler/Taypotat — does the law create a distinction based on enumerated/analogous ground? Does it impose a burden or deny a benefit in a manner that reinforces disadvantage?

criminal-law.name: Criminal Law
keyFrameworks: Elements of a crime (actus reus + mens rea)
Modes of participation (principal, aiding, abetting, counselling)
Defences (self-defence s.34, duress s.17, necessity, provocation, intoxication)
criminal-law.systemPromptAddition: Core frameworks: (1) Actus reus: voluntary act or omission (where duty exists) causing prohibited consequence. Mens rea: subjective (intention, knowledge, recklessness, wilful blindness) vs objective (criminal negligence — marked departure from standard of reasonable person). (2) Self-defence (s.34 Criminal Code, post-2012): reasonable belief of force/threat + act committed for purpose of defending + act is reasonable in the circumstances. (3) Duress (s.17 for principals — narrow statutory defence; common law for parties — Ryan). (4) Necessity (Perka): imminent peril, no reasonable legal alternative, proportionality between harm avoided and harm inflicted. (5) Murder: s.229(a) — intentional killing or intentional bodily harm likely to cause death with recklessness. First degree: planned and deliberate, or s.231 categories. (6) Charter: s.8 search and seizure (Hunter v Southam — reasonable expectation of privacy), s.9 arbitrary detention, s.10(b) right to counsel (Brydges), s.24(2) exclusion of evidence (Grant test).

foundations-of-canadian-law.name: Foundations of Canadian Law
keyFrameworks: Sources of Canadian law (Constitution, statute, common law, Indigenous law)
Rule of law and constitutional supremacy
Federalism and division of powers overview
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms overview
foundations-of-canadian-law.systemPromptAddition: Core frameworks: (1) Driedger modern principle of statutory interpretation: the words of an Act are to be read in their entire context, in their grammatical and ordinary sense harmoniously with the scheme of the Act, the object of the Act, and the intention of Parliament (Rizzo & Rizzo Shoes). (2) Sources of law hierarchy: Constitution (supreme law — s.52(1) Constitution Act, 1982), federal/provincial statutes, regulations, common law. (3) Stare decisis: courts bound by decisions of higher courts in same hierarchy; SCC binds all; horizontal stare decisis (same level — generally follow but not absolutely bound). (4) Indigenous legal orders: pre-existing sovereignty, s.35 Aboriginal rights, duty to consult (Haida Nation), UNDRIP, reconciliation framework. (5) Rule of law: Roncarelli v Duplessis — government must act within legal authority; no one above the law; law must be accessible and intelligible.

professional-responsibility.name: Professional Responsibility
keyFrameworks: Duty of loyalty and fiduciary obligations
Conflict of interest (current client, former client, personal interest)
Duty to the court vs duty to client
professional-responsibility.systemPromptAddition: Core frameworks: (1) Model Code (FLSC): governs professional conduct — adopted with variations by provincial law societies. Key rules: 3.1 (competence), 3.2 (quality of service), 3.3 (confidentiality), 3.4 (conflicts), 5.1 (duty as advocate). (2) Confidentiality (Rule 3.3): near-absolute duty; exceptions: future harm exception (imminent risk of death or serious bodily harm), innocence at stake, legal requirement. Solicitor-client privilege: evidentiary rule, belongs to client, survives termination. (3) Conflicts (Rule 3.4): current client conflicts — cannot act against current client even in unrelated matter without informed consent; former client conflicts (Neil/McKercher test) — substantially related matters. (4) Duty to court (Rule 5.1): cannot knowingly assist/permit client to present false evidence; must disclose adverse authority; candour with the court. Balancing: duty to client (zealous advocacy) vs duty to court (officer of the court). (5) Competence: knowledge, skill, and judgment; duty to decline or withdraw if unable to provide competent representation.

property.name: Property Law
keyFrameworks: Estates in land (fee simple, life estate, leasehold)
property.systemPromptAddition: Core frameworks: (1) Estates in land: fee simple absolute (largest estate, inheritable, alienable), life estate (measured by life of tenant — waste doctrine applies), leasehold (fixed term, periodic, at will, at sufferance). (2) Future interests: remainder (follows naturally from prior estate), reversion (returns to grantor), executory interest (cuts short prior estate). Rule against perpetuities: interest must vest within life in being + 21 years. (3) Joint tenancy: four unities required (time, title, interest, possession); right of survivorship; severance by any unilateral act. Tenancy in common: no survivorship, unequal shares permitted. (4) Easements: dominant and servient tenements; creation by express grant, implied (necessity, common intention), prescription (20 years). (5) Restrictive covenants: Tulk v Moxhay — covenant must touch and concern the land, must be negative, must be intended to bind successors, purchaser must have notice. (6) Land registration: Torrens system — indefeasibility of title, mirror principle, curtain principle.
